pages.name: The mean value
pages.text: Lesson 8’s current is `i = 3t²` amps from 0 s to 2 s. The reverse rule turns `3t²` into `t³`, so it moves 2³ = 8 C of charge: the area under it. A steady current moving the same 8 C in the same 2 s would be 8 ÷ 2 = 4 A, a flat rectangle with the same area. That height is the [[mean value]], the area under a graph ÷ the length of the stretch. Where the curve rises above the rectangle, the extra exactly fills the gap below it. The mean is not the ends’ average, (0 + 12) ÷ 2 = 6 A, as this curve spends most of the 2 s low down.
pages.alt: i equals 3t squared, from 0 s to 2 s. Area under the curve: 2 cubed equals 8 C. Mean: 8 C divided by 2 s equals 4 A, the same area. Not (0 plus 12) divided by 2 equals 6 A, the ends’ average

pages.name: A mean current
pages.task: The current `i = t²` amps, an example, flows from 0 s to 3 s. The reverse rule turns `t²` into `t³ ÷ 3`, so it moves 3³ ÷ 3 = 9 C. What is its mean current?
pages.why: Spread the 9 C over the 3 s: 9 ÷ 3 = 3 A, the height of the flat rectangle with the same area. (0 + 9) ÷ 2 = 4.5 A is the ends’ average, too high, as the curve spends most of the 3 s low down. 9 A forgets to divide by the 3 s.
pages.alt: i equals t squared, from 0 s to 3 s. 9 C spread over 3 s. 9 divided by 3 equals 3 A, the same area

pages.name: Mean of a sine wave
pages.text: An a.c. current flows one way, then back. A generator’s a.c. follows the shape of a sine wave, drawn here with a 10 A peak, an example. Area below the axis counts as minus, so over a whole cycle the backward half cancels the forward half and the mean is 0 A. A mean of 0 A says nothing about how big the current is, so for its size take the mean over half a cycle, where it flows one way. With equal bars that is the average of their heights: 4 bars give 6.53 A, 8 give 6.41 A and 100 give 6.37 A, 0.637 of the peak.

pages.name: Half a cycle
pages.task: A sine-wave current peaks at 20 A, an example. What is its mean over half a cycle?
pages.why: Over half a cycle a sine wave’s mean is 0.637 of its peak: 0.637 × 20 = 12.7 A, the height of the rectangle with the same area as the hump. 10 A, half the peak, leaves too little area. 0 A is the mean over a whole cycle, where the backward half cancels the forward half.
pages.alt: A sine-wave current, peak 20 A. Half-cycle mean: 0.637 of the peak. 0.637 times 20 equals 12.7 A, the same area

pages.name: Square, mean, root
pages.text: A heater’s heat goes with the current squared, so a backward current heats just as well. A steady current `I` gives a heater of resistance R the power `I²R`, so it heats the same as a changing current when `I²` equals the mean of `i²`. That steady current is the [[RMS value]], root mean square: square the graph, find its mean, then take the square root. Here a ramp, `i = 3t` amps, an example, rises to 6 A in 2 s and drops back. Its square’s mean is 12 A², so its RMS value is √12 = 3.46 A, more than its 3 A mean, as squaring makes the big currents count for more. Any ramp gives its peak ÷ √3.
pages.alt: A ramp, i equals 3t, and its square. Mean: half times 2 times 6 equals 6 C, divided by 2 s equals 3 A. Square 9t squared adds up to 3 times 2 cubed equals 24. Mean square: 24 divided by 2 equals 12 A squared. RMS: root 12 equals 3.46 A, or 6 divided by 1.732. Any ramp i equals A times t divided by T: mean square A squared divided by 3

pages.name: A steeper ramp
pages.task: A ramp current, `i = 6t` amps, rises from 0 to 12 A in 2 s, an example, then drops back. Its square, `36t²`, adds up to 12 × 2³ = 96 over the 2 s. What is its RMS value?
pages.why: The mean of the square is 96 ÷ 2 = 48 A², so the RMS value is √48 = 6.93 A, the same as the peak ÷ √3, 12 ÷ 1.732. 6 A is the plain mean, with no squaring. 48 is the mean square, in A², still waiting for its square root.
pages.alt: A ramp, i equals 6t, and its square. Mean square: 96 divided by 2 equals 48 A squared. RMS: root 48 equals 6.93 A

pages.name: The fold
pages.text: The sine wave’s square runs between 0 and 100 A², and its humps above 50 A² are its dips turned upside down. As the fold slides across, each hump moves a quarter cycle along, turns over and drops exactly into the dip there, leaving a flat band at 50 A², the mean square. Its root, √50 = 7.07 A, is the RMS value, the peak ÷ √2. One way to picture why it fits: a sine wave is the height of a point going steadily round a circle of radius 10. A quarter turn later its height is what its sideways distance was, and by Pythagoras height² + sideways distance² = 100, so the square now and the square a quarter cycle on always add up to 100.
pages.alt: The sine wave, 10 A peak, and its square. Square now plus square a quarter cycle on equals 100. Folded: a flat band at 50 A squared, the mean. RMS: root 50 equals 7.07 A, the peak divided by root 2. 10 divided by 1.414 equals 7.07 A: 0.707 of the peak

pages.name: A sine voltage
pages.task: A sine-wave voltage peaks at 100 V, an example. What is its RMS value?
pages.why: For a sine wave the RMS value is the peak ÷ √2, 0.707 of the peak: 100 × 0.707 = 70.7 V. 63.7 V is its mean over half a cycle, 0.637 × 100, not the RMS. 50 V divides the peak by 2 instead of by √2.

pages.text: Three waves side by side: half a cycle of a square wave of ±10 A, an example, and of the sine wave with its 10 A peak, and the ramp rising to 6 A. Under each are its mean and its RMS value, and RMS ÷ mean is called the [[form factor]]. The square wave’s size is always 10 A, so its mean and its RMS value are both 10 A: 10 ÷ 10 = 1. The sine wave’s is 7.07 ÷ 6.37 = 1.11 and the ramp’s 3.46 ÷ 3 = 1.15. The other way round, a sine wave’s peak is 1.414 × its RMS value.

pages.task: The ramp `i = 6t`, rising to 12 A in 2 s, has a mean of 6 A and an RMS value of 6.93 A. What is its form factor?
pages.why: The form factor is the RMS value ÷ the mean value: 6.93 ÷ 6 = 1.15, the same as the 6 A ramp’s. 0.87 is 6 ÷ 6.93, the division upside down. 0.58 is 6.93 ÷ 12, the RMS value ÷ the peak.

pages.name: From RMS to peak
pages.task: A sine-wave current has an RMS value of 5 A, an example. What is its peak?
pages.why: A sine wave’s peak is 1.414 × its RMS value: 5 × 1.414 = 7.07 A. 3.54 A is 5 ÷ 1.414, which goes from a peak to an RMS value, the wrong way. 10 A doubles it, and a 10 A peak has an RMS value of 7.07 A, not 5 A.

pages.name: A sawtooth
pages.task: A sawtooth voltage rises steadily from 0 V to 30 V in a time `T`, drops back at once and repeats, an example. What is its RMS value?
pages.why: Each tooth is a ramp from 0 to its peak, so its RMS value is the peak ÷ √3: 30 ÷ 1.732 = 17.3 V. 21.2 V is 30 ÷ 1.414, the sine wave’s rule, used on a wave that is not a sine wave. 15 V is the plain mean, 30 ÷ 2, with no squaring.
